sources.title: Transparent reindexing, information-loss, task and physical-time derivations
sources.details: For T>0 and feature vectors x_t in R^B, μ_b=(1/T)Σ_{t=0}^{T-1}x_{t,b}. For reversal r(t)=T−1−t, μ′_b=(1/T)Σ_t x_{r(t),b}=μ_b by reindexing the same T terms. This is an exact-real arithmetic identity. It retains average log features because x_t=log(max(bank*|STFT_t|²,1e-8)); it is not log of mean power. If y(x) says which group comes first and y(reverse(x)) differs, any deterministic downstream function g(μ) must return the same value on identical μ, so it cannot answer both correctly using only the mean. Floating reduction artifacts are not a stable intended order code. For supervised order answering the target labels must actually distinguish the required answers; representation and label availability do not guarantee learning. A possible order-free presence task can distinguish a toy low-only sequence [(1,0),(1,0)] with mean (1,0) from a low/high sequence [(1,0),(0,1)] with mean (0.5,0.5), while its reversal has the same latter mean. This only establishes possible retained evidence, not universal detectability. Ordinal sequence [low,high] can refer to 0.1-second or 1-second intervals, or be shifted by any common offset; order alone cannot recover duration or absolute milliseconds. Physical time needs rate/hop and/or explicit interval/offset metadata. ASR targets the ordered spoken transcript; a downstream intent mapping can be many-to-one: a hand-defined rule returning 退貨 whenever the string contains 退貨 maps both 我要退貨 and one-character-error 我耍退貨 to the same answer. Thus a transcript error alone does not logically imply an intent-answer error. These are hand derivations, not measurements of a trained model.
